The War of the Breton Succession (1341–1365) was a civil conflict within the Duchy of Brittany arising from the death of Duke John III on 30 April 1341 without a direct heir, sparking rival claims to the ducal throne.\[1\] The primary contestants were Charles de Blois, husband of John III's niece Jeanne de Penthièvre and supported by King Philip VI of France, versus John de Montfort, the duke's half-brother backed by King Edward III of England.\[2\] This dynastic struggle rapidly escalated into a proxy theater of the ongoing Hundred Years' War, drawing in Anglo-French rivalries and mercenary forces across Breton territory.\[3\] John de Montfort initially seized Nantes and proclaimed himself duke, but French forces captured him in December 1341, leaving his wife, Joanna of Flanders, to lead the Montfortist resistance.\[2\] Joanna's defense of Hennebont in 1342 against a French siege exemplified determined leadership, including her famous sortie that repelled attackers and involved guerrilla tactics.\[2\] Meanwhile, Charles de Blois, recognized as duke by French authorities, advanced Penthièvre claims through military campaigns and charters, though his capture at the Battle of La Roche-Derrien in 1347 temporarily stalled French efforts.\[3\] The war featured episodic truces amid broader Anglo-French hostilities, but intermittent Breton engagements, such as the celebrated Combat of the Thirty in 1351—a chivalric duel between Anglo-Breton and Franco-Breton knights—highlighted the conflict's feudal character.\[1\] The decisive turning point came at the [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) on 29 September 1364, where Montfort forces under John de Montfort's son (the future John IV) and English commander [Sir John Chandos](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_Chandos) routed Charles de Blois's army, resulting in Charles's death and the collapse of the Penthièvre cause.\[1\] The subsequent [Treaty of Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande) in April 1365 confirmed John IV as Duke of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), though Jeanne de Penthièvre retained a nominal title and pension, preserving some Penthièvre influence.\[2\] This resolution temporarily aligned [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) with [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) but underscored the duchy's strategic value, as future successions continued to invite foreign interference until its eventual union with [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France).\[3\] The war's integration with the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War) amplified its impact, fostering [routiers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Routiers) (mercenary bands) that ravaged the countryside and complicating regional loyalties.\[1\]

Historical Context
------------------

### The Duchy of Brittany Before 1341

The Duchy of Brittany emerged from the settlement of [Celtic Britons](https://grokipedia.com/page/Celtic_Britons) in [Armorica](https://grokipedia.com/page/Armorica) during the 5th and 6th centuries AD, fleeing Anglo-Saxon invasions in [Britain](https://grokipedia.com/page/Britain) and preserving a distinct Brythonic [language](https://grokipedia.com/page/Language) and cultural traditions amid the Frankish conquest of [Gaul](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gaul).\[4\] By the [9th century](https://grokipedia.com/page/9th_century), under Nominoë and his successors, the region consolidated into a duchy with de facto independence, resisting full integration into the Carolingian and later Capetian realms through military victories and assertions of local [sovereignty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sovereignty).\[5\] Although dukes rendered homage to French kings—typically liege homage for the duchy since the [11th century](https://grokipedia.com/page/11th_century) under figures like Alan IV—their authority rested on [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) customary [law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Customary_law), including assemblies of barons and [clergy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Clergy) for counsel on taxation and war, fostering semi-autonomy despite nominal feudal overlordship.\[6\] This balance enabled Brittany to cultivate economic and diplomatic ties with [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England), exchanging [salt](https://grokipedia.com/page/Salt), [canvas](https://grokipedia.com/page/Canvas) sails, and [hemp](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hemp) for English wool and cloth via ports like [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), [Vannes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Vannes), and [Morlaix](https://grokipedia.com/page/Morlaix), which handled growing Atlantic commerce by the early [14th century](https://grokipedia.com/page/14th_century).\[7\] Agricultural output from inland manors, including [wheat](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wheat), [rye](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rye), and livestock on fertile coastal plains, supported a [population](https://grokipedia.com/page/Population) of approximately 800,000 by 1300, while [salt](https://grokipedia.com/page/Salt) production from coastal marshes near [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande) generated significant revenue through export.\[7\] These assets made the [duchy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy) a strategic buffer and prize in Anglo-French rivalries, with dukes like John II leveraging cross-Channel marriages to secure English earldoms such as [Richmond](https://grokipedia.com/page/Richmond). John III acceded in 1312 upon the death of his father Arthur II, ruling until 30 April 1341 as a peer of [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France) while bolstering legitimacy through noble alliances and pious foundations, such as a [chapel](https://grokipedia.com/page/Chapel) near [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes).\[8\] Childless after marriages to Marie of [Luxembourg](https://grokipedia.com/page/Luxembourg) (d. 1324) and Isabella de Valois (m. 1330), he governed peacefully for nearly three decades, avoiding major internal revolts by deferring to influential baronial [estates](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Estates) like those of Rohan and Penthièvre for administrative and judicial decisions.\[8\]\[9\] In 1334, [Edward](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward) III granted him the Earldom of [Richmond](https://grokipedia.com/page/Richmond), reinforcing English commercial and feudal links without immediate conflict.\[8\] This era of stability masked underlying tensions from the duke's lack of direct heirs, heightening reliance on customary [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) [estates](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Estates) to maintain cohesion amid the duchy's fragmented lordships.\[9\]

### Brittany's Position in the Anglo-French Rivalry

The outbreak of hostilities between [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) and [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France) in [1337](https://grokipedia.com/page/1337), precipitated by [Edward](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward) III's assertion of his claim to the French throne and his refusal to perform liege homage to Philip VI for the [Duchy of Aquitaine](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy_of_Aquitaine), elevated Brittany's geopolitical significance as a semi-autonomous buffer region with extensive Atlantic coastlines ideal for naval operations and cross-Channel raids.\[10\] The duchy, while nominally a [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) [fief](https://grokipedia.com/page/fief) requiring homage from its duke, had long maintained high degrees of internal [autonomy](https://grokipedia.com/page/autonomy), with its [nobility](https://grokipedia.com/page/nobility) resisting encroachments that might subordinate Breton institutions to Capetian centralization.\[1\] This structural independence, rooted in Brittany's distinct [Celtic](https://grokipedia.com/page/Celtic) heritage and fragmented baronial landscape, positioned the region as a natural arena for proxy maneuvering, where control over its ports and resources could tip the balance in the escalating Anglo-French contest for dominance in [western Europe](https://grokipedia.com/page/Western_Europe).\[11\] Brittany's barons, organized through assemblies like the _États de Bretagne_, exhibited divided loyalties shaped by pragmatic concerns for preserving local privileges against the perceived threat of fuller integration into the French realm, a dynamic exacerbated by the Valois monarchy's expanding fiscal and judicial demands. Many nobles, wary of Philip VI's growing authority, favored alliances that safeguarded ducal sovereignty, viewing English overtures as a counterweight to French [suzerainty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Suzerainty) rather than ideological alignment.\[11\] This internal fragmentation—evident in pre-1341 factionalism among high aristocracy—mirrored broader tensions, as Edward III cultivated potential Breton sympathizers through diplomatic envoys and promises of autonomy, while Philip VI enforced feudal obligations to bind the duchy closer to [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris). The barons' preference for equilibrium over subjugation stemmed from historical precedents, such as earlier dukes' successful assertions of [independence](https://grokipedia.com/page/Independence) during Plantagenet-Capetian clashes, ensuring Brittany functioned as a contested pivot rather than a passive appendage.\[1\] Duke John III (r. 1312–1341) exemplified this balancing act through calculated diplomacy, rendering liege homage to [Philip VI](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip_VI) upon his accession while leveraging the English-held [Earldom of Richmond](https://grokipedia.com/page/Earldom_of_Richmond)—confirmed to him in 1334—to foster ties with Edward III without alienating his [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) [overlord](https://grokipedia.com/page/Overlord). His [policy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Policy) of nominal neutrality amid rising tensions avoided early entanglement, as seen in his abstention from the 1339-1340 [Low Countries](https://grokipedia.com/page/Low_Countries) campaigns, prioritizing ducal consolidation over great-power commitments. This maneuver preserved Brittany's agency until John III's childless death in 1341, at which point the latent rivalry transformed the ensuing succession dispute into a [de facto](https://grokipedia.com/page/De_facto) extension of the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War), with dynastic pretenders aligning along national lines to secure external patronage for their claims.\[12\]

The Succession Crisis
---------------------

### Death of John III and Legal Claims

[John III, Duke of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany), died on 30 April 1341 at [Caen](https://grokipedia.com/page/Caen), [Normandy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Normandy), without surviving children from any of his three marriages.\[13\]\[14\] His death without direct heirs exposed ambiguities in Breton customary inheritance law, which generally permitted female succession and representation through daughters—unlike the stricter male-only [Salic law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Salic_law) codified for Frankish lands and later emphasized in Capetian [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France)—but often favored male agnates in practice when direct male lines failed.\[13\]\[15\] The ducal estates of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) convened shortly after to adjudicate the claims, highlighting tensions between local customs allowing female-line transmission and pressures from French royal influence advocating male [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture).\[11\] The senior claim emanated from Joanna of Penthièvre (c. 1319–1384), who traced her right through her mother, Joan of Brittany, the daughter of Duke Arthur II (John III's father) and his second wife, Yolande of Dreux.\[16\] This positioned Joanna as the representative of the principal branch of the ducal house, entitled under Breton custom to inherit and convey the duchy via the female line, a principle upheld in prior Breton successions.\[15\] Joanna had married Charles de Blois, nephew of King Philip VI of France, on 4 July 1337, which aligned her claim with French interests while invoking customary rights to the full duchy rather than mere appanage lands like Penthièvre.\[17\]\[16\] Proponents argued that excluding her would undermine established precedents permitting women to hold and transmit ducal authority, as seen in the inheritance patterns of Arthur II's lineage. Opposing Joanna was John de Montfort (c. 1295–1345), the uterine half-brother of John III, born to Arthur II's third wife, Mary of Limoges.\[18\] Montfort asserted priority as the closest surviving male descendant in the direct paternal line from the ducal house, contending that Breton custom, influenced by broader feudal norms, precluded female-line inheritance in favor of male kinship to preserve the duchy’s integrity against partition or foreign sway.\[18\]\[15\] By August 1341, Montfort had proclaimed himself duke, leveraging his blood proximity to challenge the Penthièvre claim and invoking interpretations akin to semi-Salic preferences that prioritized brothers over nieces in noble Breton estates.\[19\] The rival interpretations—representation through females versus strict male agnatic descent—thus framed the legal crisis, with each side citing customary precedents amid external Anglo-French rivalries that would soon amplify the dispute.\[15\]

### Rival Factions: Blois-Penthièvre vs. Montfort

The Blois-Penthièvre faction coalesced around [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles) de Blois, husband of Joan of Penthièvre, the daughter of Guy de Penthièvre and granddaughter of Duke Arthur II through his second marriage; Joan's inheritance of extensive northern [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) [estates](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Estates), including Penthièvre itself, provided a strong territorial base for mobilizing local allegiance.\[20\] Following John de Montfort's initial seizure of [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) in May 1341, [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles) advanced into [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) with forces dispatched by [Philip](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip) VI, capturing the city after a [siege](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege) in November and securing acclamation as duke from assembled [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) [estates](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Estates), reflecting the faction's rapid consolidation of internal support.\[9\] This majority backing among the nobility—encompassing powerful houses like Rohan and Laval—stemmed from pragmatic assessments of French military superiority and economic incentives, including royal subsidies and exemptions from feudal levies, rather than abstract loyalty to legalistic claims. [Philip](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip) VI, [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles)'s uncle, formally invested him as duke on 7 August 1341, dispatching 4,000 men-at-arms under French captains to enforce the alliance and deter English encroachment.\[21\] In contrast, the Montfort faction, headed by John de Montfort—whose claim derived from his marriage to [Beatrice](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beatrice), another descendant in the ducal line through a collateral branch—initially commanded minority adherence among Breton nobles, limited to coastal interests wary of [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) overreach and opportunistic mercenaries.\[9\] John de Montfort's swift actions post-30 April 1341, including homage from the estates at [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) on 20 May, briefly positioned him as interim [duke](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duke), but defections mounted as [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) power materialized, underscoring nobles' preference for viable protectors over unproven kinship. His wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders), emerged as a pivotal figure, leveraging her Nevers inheritance for funds and rallying holdouts through personal diplomacy and appeals to autonomy against Capetian dominance. Edward III of England recognized Montfort's claim by October 1341, offering naval aid and subsidies in exchange for homage, framing the alliance as a bulwark against [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) expansion amid the escalating [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War).\[22\] Noble alignments in Brittany thus hinged on calculated self-interest: the Blois-Penthièvre coalition promised integration with France's resources—vital for inland lords facing feudal obligations—while Montfort's English ties appealed to maritime barons benefiting from cross-Channel commerce and exemptions from French taxes, revealing divisions as strategic gambles on great-power patrons rather than ideological commitments to [succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/Succession) principles.\[23\] This [pragmatism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pragmatism) manifested in fluid loyalties, with families like the Clissons hedging bets until outcomes clarified, prioritizing land security and fiscal relief over partisan fervor.

Outbreak of the War
-------------------

### Initial Seizures and Declarations (1341)

Following the death of Duke John III on 30 April 1341, John de Montfort rapidly asserted his claim to the duchy by marching to [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), the capital, with a force of approximately 200 men and taking possession without opposition in early summer. He subsequently secured the ducal treasury at [Limoges](https://grokipedia.com/page/Limoges) and occupied several other strategic strongholds across [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), thereby establishing de facto control over much of the territory in the initial weeks of the crisis.\[9\]\[24\] An assembly of Breton notables convened shortly thereafter and overwhelmingly favored the rival claim of Charles de Blois, backed by the powerful Penthièvre family and aligned with French interests, reflecting the preference for [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture) through the female line under prevailing Breton customs. King [Philip VI of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip_VI_of_France), whose sister [Margaret of Valois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Margaret_of_Valois) was Charles's mother, endorsed this position, viewing Montfort's actions as a challenge to royal authority and feudal overlordship. On 30 September 1341, the Court of Peers of France formally declared Charles de Blois the rightful duke, citing both Breton succession norms and French legal precedents that prioritized the Blois-Penthièvre lineage.\[11\]\[25\] Montfort's refusal to acknowledge these declarations prompted Philip VI to summon him to [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris) under the pretense of homage, but en route or upon initial French military pressure, Montfort's position unraveled; he was captured at [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) amid the escalating tensions, and imprisoned in the [Louvre](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louvre), marking the collapse of early diplomatic overtures. While most Breton lords acquiesced to Blois's claim, pockets of localized resistance persisted in areas loyal to Montfort, particularly in the northwest, underscoring the incomplete nature of the endorsements and setting the stage for broader conflict despite appeals for [arbitration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Arbitration) that yielded no resolution.\[18\]\[11\]

### Siege of Nantes and Montfort's Imprisonment

In late October 1341, following John de Montfort's proclamation as duke and his seizure of [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) as a key stronghold, a French royal army under the command of Charles de Blois advanced into eastern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) to enforce Philip VI's support for Blois's claim. Montfort's forces had suffered a prior defeat at the Battle of Champtoceaux in September, weakening their position and allowing the besiegers to invest [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) with superior numbers, including French troops and Breton allies loyal to Blois. The siege relied primarily on encirclement and blockade to cut off supplies, rather than immediate assault, exploiting the city's isolation and Montfort's limited garrison.\[26\] After approximately three weeks, on November 21, 1341, the citizens of [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) surrendered the city to Charles de Blois, delivering Montfort into captivity amid reports of internal pressure or negotiation under false promises of [safe conduct](https://grokipedia.com/page/Safe_conduct). This capitulation reflected divided loyalties within the city, where some residents favored reconciliation with French-backed forces to avoid prolonged starvation or destruction, effectively betraying Montfort despite his initial popular support in the region. Montfort was transported to [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris) and imprisoned in the [Louvre](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louvre), sidelining him from the conflict for several years and depriving the Montfort faction of its primary military leader.\[27\] The capture created an immediate leadership vacuum in the Montfortist cause, which his wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders), rapidly filled in early 1342 by declaring their infant son, John, as the rightful duke and assuming regency. Joan mobilized remaining supporters, securing control of towns like [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes) and initiating recruitment to counter Blois's advances, thereby preserving Montfort's claim through her active command until English intervention could materialize.\[28\]\[29\]

Early Phases and English Involvement (1342–1347)
------------------------------------------------

### Defense of Hennebont by Joan of Flanders

In late May 1342, following the capture of [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes), Charles de Blois advanced on Hennebont, a fortified port town in southern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) where [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders), acting as regent for her imprisoned husband John de Montfort, had gathered supporters and supplies.\[30\] De Blois's army, numbering several thousand including French reinforcements under Louis of Spain, established a [blockade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blockade) by land and sea, employing [siege](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege) engines, mining operations, and bombardment to breach the walls defended by a [garrison](https://grokipedia.com/page/Garrison) of roughly 500 men. Joan, demonstrating resolve amid dwindling resources, personally commanded the defense, donning armor and wielding a [sword](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sword) to rally troops and civilians, including exhorting women to arm themselves by shortening skirts for mobility and fighting alongside men.\[30\] \[2\] A pivotal moment came during a nocturnal [sortie](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sortie) organized by Joan, in which she dispatched three small ships laden with combustibles—[pitch](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pitch), [brimstone](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brimstone), and [flax](https://grokipedia.com/page/Flax)—ignited and directed toward the anchored [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) vessels in the harbor.\[30\] These fire ships, manned by volunteers including crossbowmen, collided with and set ablaze several of de Blois's larger transports, disrupting the naval blockade and inflicting material losses estimated at a dozen vessels, though exaggerated in contemporary accounts like those of [Jean Froissart](https://grokipedia.com/page/Jean_Froissart).\[30\] \[31\] The [raid](https://grokipedia.com/page/Raid), conducted under cover of darkness, not only damaged enemy logistics but also exemplified Joan's adoption of guerrilla tactics, compensating for numerical inferiority through audacity and surprise.\[2\] English intervention proved decisive; in early June, a contingent of 234 men-at-arms led by Sir Walter Manny, dispatched by Edward III, landed nearby and conducted harassing raids on de Blois's encampment, forcing the besiegers to divide forces and exposing supply lines. Overwhelmed by this external pressure and repeated repulses—including failed assaults on the walls—Manny's presence compelled de Blois to lift the siege by late June, withdrawing northward without capturing the town.\[30\] Joan's tenacious stand at Hennebont, earning her the epithet _Jeanne la Flamme_ for its ferocity, preserved a critical Montfort stronghold and sustained factional resistance against de Blois's initial dominance, which had secured much of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) earlier that year.\[30\] By holding out through personal leadership and opportunistic strikes, she forestalled a potential collapse of the pro-Montfort cause, bolstering [morale](https://grokipedia.com/page/Morale) among allies and drawing further English commitment to the Breton theater amid the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War).\[2\] \[31\] This defense underscored the war's reliance on localized fortifications and naval elements, preventing de Blois from consolidating gains before broader Anglo-Breton coordination intensified.

### Battle of La Roche-Derrien

The Battle of La Roche-Derrien occurred on the night of 18–19 June 1347, during the Breton War of Succession, as part of English efforts to support John de Montfort's claim against Charles de Blois, backed by France. Charles de Blois, with an army of approximately 4,000–5,000 troops including 1,800 men-at-arms, 2,000 crossbowmen, and 600 archers, laid siege to the town of La Roche-Derrien in May 1347, which was held by an English garrison loyal to Montfort. The siege aimed not primarily to capture the town but to draw out Sir Thomas Dagworth, the English commander in Brittany, into a pitched battle where Blois's superior numbers could prevail.\[32\]\[33\]\[34\] Dagworth, leading a force of about 700–800 men primarily composed of English longbowmen and men-at-arms, marched to relieve the [garrison](https://grokipedia.com/page/Garrison) but opted for a surprise night assault on Blois's encampment rather than a direct confrontation. Approaching under cover of darkness, Dagworth's troops exploited the disorganization in the enemy camp, where soldiers were resting without full readiness. English archers unleashed volleys that caused panic among the besiegers, allowing men-at-arms to close in and engage in [melee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Melee); the attack enveloped parts of Blois's lines, leading to heavy [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) and [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) casualties as units fragmented in the confusion.\[32\]\[35\] The battle resulted in a decisive English tactical victory, with [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois)'s army suffering significant losses, including the deaths of several Breton and French nobles, and the wounding and capture of Charles de [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) himself, who was taken prisoner by Dagworth's forces. English casualties were relatively light, though exact figures remain uncertain. This outcome disrupted [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois)'s military operations in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), temporarily shifting momentum toward the Montfort-English alliance amid broader English successes in the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War), such as the recent victory at Crécy in 1346, and hampering French-Breton coordination in the region.\[32\]\[33\]

Mid-War Stalemate and Captivities (1347–1357)
---------------------------------------------

### Temporary Capture of Charles de Blois

Charles de Blois was captured during the night assault at the [Battle of La Roche-Derrien](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_La_Roche-Derrien) on 20 June 1347, when English and Montfortist forces under Sir Thomas Dagworth surprised his encampment. Found unarmoured and wounded 17 times in his tent, Blois was taken prisoner by Dagworth and transported to [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England), where he was confined in various castles before incarceration in the [Tower of London](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tower_of_London).\[32\] He remained a captive for nine years until his release in August 1356, following protracted [ransom](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ransom) negotiations that culminated in a payment of approximately 500,000 to 700,000 écus or florins, though exact figures varied in contemporary accounts.\[36\]\[37\] Blois's capture severely undermined the Blois-Penthièvre claim, depriving the French-backed faction of its central figure and prompting King [Philip VI of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip_VI_of_France) to lose his primary ducal candidate in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany). His wife, [Joanna](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna) of Penthièvre, assumed leadership of their remaining forces, but the absence of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) hampered coordinated offensives and shifted momentum toward the English-allied Montfortists.\[32\] The English briefly retained control of La Roche-Derrien, though French forces later recaptured it, massacring many inhabitants in reprisal.\[32\] The Montfort faction exploited Blois's captivity to secure recognition from Breton estates and expand influence, with [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders) and her son—the future John V—acknowledged as the legitimate duchess and heir under English protection. However, these gains proved constrained by the prior death of John de Montfort in September 1345, which had placed the six-year-old heir under regency and English guardianship, limiting decisive leadership and aggressive campaigns to fully consolidate advantages.\[19\]\[32\] Blois's prolonged imprisonment induced a temporary lull in major hostilities within Brittany, as both sides maneuvered amid the broader truces of the Hundred Years' War, stalling the succession conflict until his return reinvigorated Penthièvre efforts.\[38\]

### Impact of Broader Truces in the Hundred Years' War

The Truce of Calais, concluded on 28 September 1347 between Edward III of England and Philip VI of France following the English capture of Calais, imposed a nine-month cessation of hostilities that was repeatedly extended until 1355, effectively constraining major Anglo-French military engagements across the broader Hundred Years' War. This external restraint directly contributed to a prolonged stalemate in the War of the Breton Succession, as it limited the influx of reinforcements and resources from both crowns to their respective Breton proxies—John de Montfort for England and Charles de Blois for France—preventing decisive escalations and reducing the conflict to sporadic guerrilla actions, raids, and localized sieges rather than coordinated campaigns. Although Blois invoked the truce's inapplicability to his "private" dynastic claim, the absence of large-scale foreign support fostered a de-escalatory impasse, with Montfort's forces holding key coastal enclaves while Blois maintained inland strongholds, underscoring how supranational truces subordinated regional proxy wars to diplomatic imperatives.\[39\] Breton barons, prioritizing local autonomy over unwavering loyalty to either claimant, exploited these truces to hedge allegiances, frequently shifting support between Blois and Montfort factions to negotiate favorable terms, extract concessions, or evade domination by [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) or English overlords. Such opportunism, evident in documented defections among [nobility](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nobility) like those aligned with the Penthièvre family, reflected a strategic [calculus](https://grokipedia.com/page/Calculus) where barons leveraged the stalemate to preserve feudal privileges amid uncertain outcomes, often switching sides during lulls in 1347–1350 to secure exemptions from taxation or military obligations. This fluidity undermined cohesive strategies for either claimant, perpetuating fragmentation and ensuring no faction achieved [hegemony](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hegemony) without external [royal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Royal) intervention.\[1\] The economic ramifications of these truce-enforced stalemates exacerbated Brittany's rural devastation, as intermittent raiding and supply disruptions persisted without resolution, leading to agricultural decline, disrupted trade routes, and heightened taxation burdens on peasantry to sustain fragmented garrisons. Countryside depopulation accelerated due to ongoing [low-intensity conflict](https://grokipedia.com/page/Low-intensity_conflict), with fields left [fallow](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fallow) and villages abandoned, compounding the broader Hundred Years' War's fiscal strains without yielding territorial gains or reconstruction. This pattern of attrition, devoid of conclusive victories, imposed a heavier toll than intermittent full-scale warfare, as prolonged uncertainty deterred investment and perpetuated subsistence-level economies across Breton lordships.\[40\]

Resumed Hostilities and Climax (1357–1364)
------------------------------------------

### Release of Combatants and Renewed Campaigns

Charles de Blois, claimant to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy_of_Brittany) and supported by the French crown, was released from English captivity in the [Tower of London](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tower_of_London) in 1356 after his forces paid a ransom of approximately 500,000 écus.\[36\] His nine-year imprisonment, stemming from capture at the [Battle of La Roche-Derrien](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_La_Roche-Derrien) in 1347, had stalled French-backed efforts, but his freedom reinvigorated the Blois faction amid fragile truces in the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War). De Blois promptly resumed command, leveraging renewed French logistical and military aid to launch raids and consolidate holdings in eastern and northern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), where loyalties remained divided.\[19\] Bertrand du Guesclin, a rising [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) captain aligned with French interests, emerged as a key commander for de [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) during this phase, employing irregular tactics to harass English garrisons and supply lines. In late 1356 to early 1357, du Guesclin contributed to the defense of [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes) against an English siege led by Henry of Grosmont, [Duke of Lancaster](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duke_of_Lancaster), who sought to bolster Montfort partisans; the six-month operation ended inconclusively with English withdrawal following French relief efforts and seasonal pressures. This period marked escalating cross-border raids, with du Guesclin coordinating small-scale chevauchées to reclaim outlying fortresses and disrupt Montfort-aligned commerce, foreshadowing larger offensives by 1362.\[41\] On the Montfort side, English-backed forces maintained a network of coastal strongholds like [Brest](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brest) and Hennebont, from which they launched punitive chevauchées into Blois-controlled territories to counter de Blois's resurgence. The young John de Montfort, heir to the English-favored claim and residing in exile in [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) since childhood, coordinated indirectly through royal patronage; King [Edward](https://grokipedia.com/page/King_Edward) III authorized reinforcements and subsidies to sustain Montfort captains, preventing total collapse despite de Blois's momentum. These reciprocal raids devastated rural economies and fortified positions, prolonging the stalemate while broader English successes—such as the Black Prince's 1356 campaign culminating at [Poitiers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Poitiers)—diverted French resources away from [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany).\[19\]

### Battle of Auray and Death of Charles de Blois

The [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) was fought on 29 September 1364 near the town of [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray) in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), pitting the forces of John de Montfort, supported by English commanders including [Sir John Chandos](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_Chandos), Robert Knolles, and Sir Hugh Calveley, against the army of Charles de Blois led by [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bertrand_du_Guesclin) and Jean de Chalon.\[42\] Montfort's army numbered approximately 2,000 men, while Blois commanded 3,000 to 4,000 troops.\[42\] The Montfortists positioned themselves defensively along a stream and marshy ground to protect their flanks, deploying dismounted men-at-arms in the center flanked by English longbowmen, a tactic proven effective in prior engagements of the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War).\[43\]\[42\] Du Guesclin, seeking to counter the English [archery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Archery) advantage, advanced his men-at-arms on foot behind large [pavise](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pavise) shields to minimize arrow casualties, an adaptation that limited initial losses from [longbow](https://grokipedia.com/page/Longbow) fire.\[43\] However, this approach proved inflexible in the ensuing [hand-to-hand combat](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hand-to-hand_combat), where the Montfortist center held firm under Chandos' command on the right wing, bolstered by concentrated archer volleys that disrupted [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois)' formations.\[43\]\[42\] Tactical errors compounded the Bloisists' disadvantages, including desertions by [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) contingents unwilling to fight fellow [Bretons](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bretons), which weakened their lines before [melee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Melee) engagement.\[42\] As the battle progressed into close quarters, the fall of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois)' standard triggered a [rout](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rout) among his forces, during which Charles de [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) himself was killed in the [melee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Melee), shattering the French-backed claimant's [leadership](https://grokipedia.com/page/Leadership).\[42\] Du Guesclin was captured amid the [collapse](https://grokipedia.com/page/Collapse), underscoring the failure of the [pavise](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pavise) tactic to translate into victory despite reducing [archery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Archery) impacts.\[43\] Casualties were heavily lopsided: the Anglo-Breton side suffered fewer than 100 dead, including only 7 men-at-arms, while [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois)' army incurred around 800 killed and 1,200 captured, decisively tilting control of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) toward Montfort.\[42\] The English longbowmen's role in breaking formations and exploiting the [rout](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rout) proved pivotal, reinforcing the tactical superiority of [combined arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/Combined_arms) over rigid [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) advances.\[43\]\[42\]

Resolution
----------

### Treaty of Guérande (1365)

The First Treaty of Guérande, signed on 12 April 1365 at the Château de Suscinio near [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande), formally ended the War of the Breton Succession by recognizing John IV de Montfort as the legitimate Duke of Brittany.\[1\] This agreement followed the decisive Montfort victory at the [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) on 29 September 1364, where rival claimant Charles de Blois was killed, compelling King [Charles V](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles_V) of France to concede despite his prior endorsement of the Blois-Penthièvre faction.\[12\] The treaty's terms prioritized Montfort consolidation of power, excluding Blois heirs from ducal succession while mandating John IV's personal homage to [Charles V](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles_V) as overlord, a nominal restoration of French [suzerainty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Suzerainty) weakened by defeats in the broader [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War).\[21\] Joanna de Penthièvre, Charles de Blois's widow and co-heiress, was compelled to renounce her claims to the duchy, signing the treaty under duress after her husband's death and the collapse of French-backed resistance.\[21\] In compensation, she retained lifelong possession of extensive appanages including the counties of Penthièvre and Avaugour, along with an annual pension of 40,000 francs paid by the [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) duke, but her descendants were explicitly barred from inheriting the ducal title.\[21\] These provisions secured Penthièvre economic influence without threatening Montfort rule, reflecting pragmatic French concessions to stabilize the frontier amid ongoing English alliances. The treaty incorporated French reservations by requiring John IV to govern in alignment with pre-1341 customs of limited autonomy under royal oversight, though enforcement was deferred given Brittany's entrenched English ties—John IV had been raised in [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) and continued military cooperation with Edward III.\[12\] Charles V's acceptance stemmed from strategic necessity after the 1356 capture of his father John II at [Poitiers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Poitiers) and Breton exhaustion, allowing temporary peace without full renunciation of overlordship; breaches could justify future intervention, as evidenced by the Second Treaty of [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande) in 1381.\[44\] This framework favored immediate Montfort ascendancy but sowed seeds of recurrent Franco-Breton tension.

### Establishment of Montfort Rule

Following the Treaty of [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande) on 12 April 1365, which formally recognized John IV de Montfort as Duke of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) and led Jeanne de Penthièvre to renounce her claims tied to the Blois pretenders, John IV entered the duchy to assert control.\[45\] \[5\] He faced pockets of resistance from holdouts loyal to the defeated Charles de Blois, whose death at the [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) on 29 September 1364 had not fully eradicated partisan strongholds.\[45\] \[5\] Through targeted military operations, John IV captured or neutralized these bastions, politically isolating and executing prominent Blois sympathizers to eliminate threats and deter further uprisings.\[5\] \[46\] To secure legitimacy amid divided noble loyalties, John IV rendered liege homage to King Charles V of [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France) on 13 December 1366, affirming French overlordship while safeguarding [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) customs and privileges.\[47\] \[5\] His prior English alliances, forged during the war and including homage to Edward III, persisted through financial ties and military pacts, enabling him to maintain the earldom of [Richmond](https://grokipedia.com/page/Richmond)—restored in July 1372 after negotiations.\[5\] \[45\] This dual homage positioned John IV to leverage both crowns against each other, preserving ducal independence without full subordination to either.\[45\] Internally, John IV implemented measures to reconcile the fractured nobility, offering pardons to lower-tier [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) adherents who swore fealty while confiscating lands from unrepentant leaders to redistribute among Montfort loyalists.\[5\] These steps, alongside early fiscal impositions to fund [reconstruction](https://grokipedia.com/page/Reconstruction), aimed to centralize authority and prevent factional resurgence, though they strained relations with tax-weary estates.\[45\] By integrating former adversaries into his administration where feasible, he fostered a fragile [equilibrium](https://grokipedia.com/page/Equilibrium) that reduced overt civil strife by the early 1370s.\[5\] English backing, crucial for his 1364 triumph, gradually diminished as John IV prioritized diplomatic maneuvering over reliance on foreign garrisons, withdrawing permissions for [English](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) troops in key fortresses to appease [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) sensitivities while covertly aiding [English](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) operations in 1370.\[45\] This shift reflected pragmatic realism: overdependence on [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) risked [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) reprisals that could undermine his freshly won [sovereignty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sovereignty), prompting a measured reorientation toward balanced suzerainties without alienating either patron.\[5\] \[45\]

Military and Strategic Analysis
-------------------------------

### Key Tactics, Battles, and Naval Actions

English forces supporting John de Montfort integrated longbowmen with dismounted men-at-arms, delivering rapid arrow volleys that disrupted enemy formations and inflicted casualties on advancing knights before melee engagement. This tactic, honed in the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War), demonstrated superiority in pitched battles by exploiting the longbow's range of up to 300 meters and fire rate of 10-12 arrows per minute per archer, outpacing French crossbowmen.\[48\]\[43\] In the Battle of Auray on 29 September 1364, Montfortist [archers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Archery) positioned on elevated ground targeted Bloisist [heavy cavalry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Heavy_cavalry), weakening charges and enabling counterattacks that shattered the opposing line, resulting in Charles de Blois's death and the rout of approximately 2,000 French-led troops against fewer than 1,000 English-allied casualties. French tactics emphasized massed knightly assaults in close order, prioritizing shock impact over missile defense, which empirically failed against prepared [archery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Archery) screens as knights dismounted or faltered under arrow storms.\[49\] The [Combat of the Thirty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Combat_of_the_Thirty) on 27 March 1351 exemplified rare foot combat without ranged weapons, where 30 Breton-French knights challenged 30 Anglo-Breton counterparts in a structured [melee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Melee) using swords, axes, and daggers; the Anglo-Bretons prevailed after four hours, killing or capturing most opponents, underscoring the vulnerability of isolated knightly virtue to coordinated group tactics amid exhaustion and wounds.\[50\] Sieges characterized much of the conflict owing to Brittany's fragmented [bocage](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bocage) terrain—dense hedges, woods, and enclosures—that hindered maneuver and favored fortified defenses, prolonging engagements through starvation and raids rather than decisive field actions; examples include the prolonged defense of Hennebont in 1342, where sorties and scorched-earth measures repelled attackers despite numerical inferiority.\[30\] Naval operations supported land campaigns via English control of sea lanes, as in the 1342 capture of [Brest](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brest) harbor, which secured a base for reinforcements and imposed blockades that starved French garrisons and disrupted coastal supply, with fleets of cogs and barges enabling amphibious landings unopposed by inferior Breton-French naval forces.\[51\]

### Comparative Strengths of English and French Support

The French Crown's support for Charles de Blois emphasized centralized command and large-scale land recruitment, drawing on feudal levies and royal armies numbering in the thousands, such as the 7,000 troops dispatched to [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) in 1341 to enforce Blois's claim.\[52\] This approach, while providing numerical superiority in conventional engagements, proved rigid due to dependence on royal directives and Blois's dynastic legitimacy through [marriage](https://grokipedia.com/page/Marriage) to Jeanne de Penthièvre, a female-line claimant whose position alienated Breton [nobles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Noble) favoring male [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture) traditions.\[19\] The tie to French overlordship further eroded local support, as it positioned Blois as a [proxy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Proxy) for Valois expansion rather than an autonomous [duke](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duke), limiting adaptability to Brittany's decentralized [noble](https://grokipedia.com/page/Noble) networks and guerrilla-style resistance.\[19\] In contrast, English backing of John de Montfort prioritized opportunistic alliances, with Edward III pledging troops, funds, and naval assets in exchange for nominal [suzerainty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Suzerainty), enabling flexible responses to fluctuating Breton needs without rigid feudal obligations.\[52\] This included deployment of professional mercenaries and commanders skilled in [irregular warfare](https://grokipedia.com/page/Irregular_warfare), better suited to Brittany's coastal and forested terrain, where small, mobile forces could exploit [hit-and-run tactics](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hit-and-run_tactics) against larger opponents.\[19\] English strategy adjusted dynamically to truces and opportunities, minimizing overcommitment while sustaining Montfortist holdouts through targeted aid rather than wholesale occupation. Resource disparities underscored these dynamics: England's established naval dominance in the [Channel](https://grokipedia.com/page/Channel) facilitated rapid reinforcements and coastal control, securing supply lines immune to French land [interdiction](https://grokipedia.com/page/Interdiction) and amplifying Montfort's defensive posture in maritime-dependent regions.\[52\] [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France), conversely, leveraged its vast manpower for land campaigns but faced logistical strains from overland mobilization across hostile territory, with rigid army structures ill-equipped for prolonged [low-intensity conflict](https://grokipedia.com/page/Low-intensity_conflict).\[19\] The English model's causal efficacy lay in its alignment with [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) autonomy preferences, allowing Montfort to cultivate indigenous alliances unburdened by perceived foreign domination, thereby offsetting initial material disadvantages through adaptive leverage rather than sheer volume.\[52\]

Aftermath and Legacy

### Effects on Breton Autonomy

The Treaty of Guérande, signed on April 12, 1365, confirmed John de Montfort's son, John V, as Duke of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), thereby resolving the [succession crisis](https://grokipedia.com/page/Succession_crisis) in favor of the Montfort claimants while stipulating the [duchy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy)'s neutrality in broader Anglo-[French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) conflicts and affirming its internal [self-governance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-governance) under nominal [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) overlordship.\[6\] This arrangement preserved [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany)'s distinct legal and administrative structures, including its customary laws and provincial [estates](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Estates), preventing immediate absorption into the [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) crown's direct domain despite the duke's obligation to render homage to the king of [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France).\[53\] The Montfort dukes leveraged this status to pursue policies of relative sovereignty, such as independent [diplomacy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Diplomacy) and fiscal [autonomy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Autonomy), which eroded ducal [absolutism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Absolutism) but shielded the duchy from full centralization for over a century.\[7\] Brittany's geopolitical position as a coastal buffer between English-held territories in [Aquitaine](https://grokipedia.com/page/Aquitaine) and the [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) heartland enabled its dukes to exploit rivalries, extracting concessions from both powers to maintain [de facto](https://grokipedia.com/page/De_facto) [independence](https://grokipedia.com/page/Independence); this balancing act delayed definitive annexation until the Edict of [Union](https://grokipedia.com/page/Union) in August 1532, when the childless death of Duchess Anne's heirs prompted formal incorporation under retained privileges.\[53\] The war's factional divisions among [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) nobles, who aligned variably with Blois-Penthièvre [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) supporters or Montfort English allies, fragmented centralized authority, empowering regional lords and [the Estates](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Estates) of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany)—a representative assembly of [clergy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Clergy), [nobility](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nobility), and third estate—to veto ducal decisions and control taxation, thereby decentralizing power and laying groundwork for recurrent assertions of provincial rights against royal encroachments.\[7\] The conflict inflicted demographic scars through sieges, battles like [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray) in 1364, and resultant famines, reducing noble lineages and rural populations, yet these losses spurred post-war consolidation under Montfort rule without collapsing the duchy's viability.\[6\] Economically, disruptions to inland agriculture and coastal raids hampered short-term output, but recovery ensued via resilient maritime commerce in salt, wine, and textiles through ports such as [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) and [Saint-Malo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Saint-Malo), bolstering fiscal independence and reinforcing Brittany's identity as a semi-autonomous entity resistant to wholesale French integration.\[7\]

### Integration into the Hundred Years' War Dynamics

The victory of John de Montfort at the [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) in 1364 solidified English influence in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), aligning the duchy as a strategic asset during the Edwardian phase of the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War), which represented the high-water mark of English territorial ambitions on the continent.\[54\] Montfort's alliance with Edward III enabled the English to leverage Breton ports, such as [Brest](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brest)—seized in 1342 and retained under pro-English control—for logistical support, including the transport of troops, supplies, and naval reinforcements to sustain operations in western [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France) following the [Treaty of Brétigny](https://grokipedia.com/page/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny) in 1360.\[51\] This access facilitated English chevauchées and garrisons, countering French efforts to isolate [Aquitaine](https://grokipedia.com/page/Aquitaine) and [Normandy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Normandy) until reversals in the late 1360s, when French forces under [Charles V](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles_V) began reclaiming territories.\[41\] Bertrand du Guesclin's survival and ransom after capture at [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray) proved pivotal for French recovery, as his subsequent appointment as [Constable of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Constable_of_France) in 1370 allowed him to orchestrate guerrilla tactics and sieges that eroded English holdings, including in Brittany-adjacent regions.\[41\] His campaigns from 1370 to 1373, emphasizing attrition over pitched battles, exploited the overextension of English [logistics](https://grokipedia.com/page/Logistics) reliant on vulnerable coastal supply lines from allied Breton bases.\[55\] Long-term, the Breton war entrenched divided loyalties within the duchy, complicating Anglo-French balances even after John IV de Montfort's pragmatic shift toward France amid Charles V's 1378 confiscation threat, culminating in the 1381 Treaty of [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande) where he pledged homage to the French crown while retaining [autonomy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Autonomy).\[53\] This realignment undermined English strategic depth in the 1380s, as Breton ports transitioned from facilitators of invasion to neutral or hostile bases, yet the precedent of Montfort's English-backed rule perpetuated Breton ambivalence, hindering full French integration until the [15th century](https://grokipedia.com/page/15th_century).\[12\]

Chronology
----------

### Timeline of Major Events

*   **30 April 1341**: Death of [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany), without male heirs, sparking the succession dispute between John de Montfort (claiming through his wife [Joanna of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders)) and Charles de Blois (claiming through his wife Joan of Penthièvre).\[56\]
*   **October 1341**: Battle of Champtoceaux results in the capture of John de Montfort by [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) forces supporting Charles de Blois.\[24\]
*   **1345**: Death of John de Montfort in Hennebont while ill, leaving his young son John as claimant under English protection.\[57\]
*   **20 June 1347**: Night battle at La Roche-Derrien sees English-Breton forces under Thomas Dagworth defeat and capture Charles de Blois.\[32\]
*   **27 March 1351**: [Combat of the Thirty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Combat_of_the_Thirty) pits thirty Anglo-Breton champions against thirty Franco-Breton knights near Ploërmel, ending in Anglo-Breton victory after prolonged melee.\[58\]
*   **29 September 1364**: [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) delivers decisive victory to John de Montfort's forces under [John Chandos](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_Chandos), resulting in the death of Charles de Blois and collapse of his claim.\[11\]
*   **12 April 1365**: First Treaty of [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande) formally ends the war, recognizing John V de Montfort as Duke of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) under nominal [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) [suzerainty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Suzerainty).\[59\]
